tagline: Rainforest, towers and two land halves
overview:
Malaysia comes in two pieces separated by about 640 kilometers of the South China Sea. Peninsular Malaysia hangs south from mainland Asia below Thailand, ending just above Singapore, while East Malaysia occupies the northern third of Borneo, the world's third largest island, alongside Indonesia and Brunei. Together they are a little larger than New Mexico. Kuala Lumpur, the capital, is known for the twin Petronas Towers, once the tallest buildings in the world.

About 34 million people live in Malaysia, and the population is a genuine mixture of Malays and Indigenous groups together with large Chinese and Indian communities whose ancestors arrived generations ago. Malay is the national language and English is widely spoken, with Mandarin, Tamil and dozens of Indigenous languages heard every day. Malaysia is a constitutional monarchy with an unusual arrangement: nine hereditary state rulers take turns as king, each serving five years. Palm oil, electronics and natural rubber drive the economy.
landAndNature: Malaysia sits just above the equator, hot and humid all year, and its rainforests are among the oldest on Earth, far older than the Amazon. Mount Kinabalu in Borneo rises to 4,095 meters, the highest peak in Southeast Asia. Mangroves and coral reefs line the coasts, and the waters off Sipadan are famous among divers. Borneo's forests shelter orangutans, pygmy elephants and proboscis monkeys with long drooping noses, while the rafflesia, the largest single flower in the world, can reach a meter across and smells of rotting meat. The caves at Gunung Mulu include a chamber big enough to swallow dozens of airliners.
peopleAndCulture: Malaysian food is one of the country's great pleasures: nasi lemak, coconut rice with chili paste, is the unofficial national dish, and roti canai, laksa noodle soup, satay skewers and Chinese noodles are sold at open-air hawker stalls at all hours. Islam is the official religion, while Buddhist, Hindu, Christian and Indigenous communities keep their own festivals, so the calendar is unusually full: Hari Raya, Chinese New Year, Deepavali and Christmas are all marked, often with open houses where neighbors of any background are welcome. Badminton is a national obsession, and sepak takraw is played with a rattan ball and no hands.
history: Trading ports flourished along the Strait of Malacca for well over a thousand years, and the Malacca Sultanate became a great center of commerce in the 1400s, spreading Islam through the region. Portugal seized Malacca in 1511, the Dutch took it in 1641, and Britain gradually gained control of the peninsula and the Borneo territories, bringing Chinese and Indian laborers to work tin mines and rubber plantations. Japan occupied the region during World War II. Malaya became independent on August 31, 1957, and in 1963 joined with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia; Singapore left two years later. Malaysia has since grown into one of Southeast Asia's stronger economies.
funFacts: Nine of Malaysia's states have hereditary rulers who take turns serving five-year terms as the country's king.
The Petronas Twin Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004 and are joined by a sky bridge.
Malaysia's rainforests are roughly 130 million years old, far older than the Amazon.
The rafflesia, found in Malaysian forests, produces the largest single flower on Earth and smells like rotting meat.
Sarawak Chamber at Gunung Mulu is among the largest cave chambers known, big enough to hold many jumbo jets.
